paragraphs.source_en: At this, Tofu struck his thigh with his hand and said in a decisive tone, "Sir, I am utterly opposed to that doctrine of yours. In my view, when one asks what is most precious in this world, I believe there is nothing more precious than love and beauty. It is wholly thanks to these two things that we receive consolation, are made complete, and attain happiness. It is also wholly by relying on these two that our sentiments become graceful, our character noble, and our sympathy purified. Therefore, whatever age or place we are born into, we cannot forget these things. Once these two things appear in the real world, love becomes the relation called husband and wife, while beauty takes the several forms of poetry and music. For that reason, I believe that so long as humanity exists upon the surface of the earth, husband and wife and art will never perish."

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, "It would be all very well if they did not perish, but as the present-day philosopher has just said, they have in fact already perished, so there is nothing for it but to resign ourselves. What is that, art? Art, too, meets the same fate as husband and wife. The development of individuality means the freedom of individuality, does it not? And the freedom of individuality means that I am I, and another person is another person, does it not? How could any such art really exist? Art flourishes because there is a common individuality between the artist and those who enjoy it. No matter how much you insist on being a poet of the new style, if there is not a single person who says your poems are interesting, then your new-style poetry, regrettably, will have no reader but yourself. What good would it do to compose any number of pieces like 'The Mandarin-Duck Song'? Fortunately you were born in this present Meiji age, and so the whole world still reads your poems fondly..."

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, "If even now they have not reached that point, then in the future, when human culture has advanced, that is, when the great philosopher appears and advocates the doctrine of non-marriage, your poems will have no readers at all. That will not, of course, be because no one reads them because you wrote them, but because each person will possess his own distinct individuality and will not find the least interest in poems or prose written by others. Even in present-day England, this tendency is already clearly visible. Among contemporary English novelists there have already appeared works with the strongest individuality; look at Meredith, look at Joyce, do they not have very few readers? Naturally they are few, for if one does not have that sort of individuality, one certainly will not find such works interesting, and there is no help for that. As this tendency gradually develops, by the time marriage has become immoral, art too will have perished altogether. Is that not so? Once the day comes when I cannot understand at all what you have written, and you cannot understand at all what I have written, then between you and me there will be no art whatsoever, will there?"
